questions.title: What is the standard of review for a District Court's summary judgment when interpreting summary judgment motions?
questions.question_body: In the Eighth Circuit's opinion, the court notes that it reviews the grant of summary judgment de novo. However, it also highlights that evidence must be viewed in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party. If summary judgment is a 'matter of law' review, why does the appellate court have to view evidence in a light favorable to the factfinder? Isn't this rule typically for the trial judge?

questions.title: Why does the Minnesota Payment of Wages Act restrict civil penalties to the Minister of Industry if the individual employee can sue for wages?
questions.question_body: The court distinguishes between rights for wages and rights for penalties under the MPWA. Section 181.101 allows 'prosecuting a claim for wages.' But for penalties, it relies on a demand by the Commissioner. How does the distinction between 'liability for civil penalties provided for in the section' and statutory demand restrict an individual employee's right to sue without administrative exhaustion?

questions.title: Why does a defendant's voluntary cessation of a violated policy trigger a mootness analysis even if the plaintiff is seeking statutory penalties rather than reduced damages?
questions.question_body: In Section II-B, the court vacates the summary judgment decision on the MFLSA claim due to a 'serious concern regarding jurisdiction.' While wages were paid and lawsuits for liquidated damages stipulated, the court worries about whether the illegal overtime practice 'could reasonably be expected to recur.' Why is the defendant's cessation of the policy relevant to the 'plaintiff's standing' for statutory penalties?

questions.title: What is the procedural standard for 'waiver of an issue' in appellate proceedings under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure?
questions.question_body: The court states that Cohen waived the issue regarding minimum wage penalties (MWTA) because the defendant's brief contained 'no meaningful argument' to support reversal. Does this mean the failure to cite statutory authority for a claim is fatal to the argument, or is it a deficiency in the briefing that prevents appellate review of a valid claim?

questions.title: Why does the appeal court lack jurisdiction over an injunctive relief claim that was withdrawn in summary judgment briefing rather than the original complaint?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that an applicant for injunctive relief must request it 'in a way that provides for appellate review.' If a party later changes their mind and requests 'affirmative injunctive order' instead of the original policy, is the claim itself barred, or is the procedural flaw the failure to reserve it in the original complaint?
